what: LEO I ran Lyons's clerical work (valuations, then payroll, orders, invoicing) in Britain.

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: LEO I ran its first business application in 1951.

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: Lyons used LEO I initially for valuation jobs, but its role was extended to include payroll, inventory, and so on.

note: Looked for earlier clerical machines: Hollerith/Powers punched-card tabulators did accounting from the 1890s-1900s, but no fetched page gave a dated billing or payroll use, and the concept is computer-based office automation (term from the 1970s). LEO I is the first computer doing routine clerical work.

what: ATR labs in Kyoto reconstructed 10x10-pixel images a person viewed from brain signals.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: allowed researchers to reconstruct images from brain signals at a resolution of 10×10 pixels

note: Earlier decoding of seen orientations (Kamitani and Tong 2005) decodes simple features, not images; Yang Dan 1999 cat thalamus is animal. Partial fit (seen images, not thoughts), but nothing earlier fits better.

what: Chang and Makin at UCSF decoded spoken sentences from ECoG signals into text.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Edward Chang and Joseph Makin from UCSF reported that ECoG signals could be used to decode speech from epilepsy patients

note: Earlier brain-to-letter systems (P300 speller 1988, Birbaumer slow-cortical-potential spelling 1999) select letters by attention or self-regulation, not by decoding thoughts, so rejected. Poor fit overall but the earliest brain-to-text decoding of language found.

what: Alvin Lucier's Music for Solo Performer (1965) used a performer's EEG alpha waves, via amplifiers and filters, to drive percussion instruments.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: one of the earliest examples of a working brain–machine interface was the piece Music for Solo Performer (1965) by American composer Alvin Lucier.

note: Wikipedia calls it a working brain-machine interface 12 years before Vidal's 1977 EEG cursor/maze demonstration (the original). It is an art piece, so the fit is arguable; Fetz 1969 monkeys and Grey Walter 1964 rejected (animal / unverified).

what: Kennedy and Bakay implanted locked-in patient Johnny Ray, who learned to control a computer cursor.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Ray's implant was installed in 1998 and he lived long enough to start working with the implant, eventually learning to control a computer cursor

note: Birbaumer's mid-1990s paralysed-patient cursor training was a lab experiment, and his spelling device is 1999; Dobelle's 1978 implant fed vision into the brain (machine to brain) and was a prototype; Dobelle's paid service is 2002. Nothing earlier found.

what: Virtuality 1000SU VR systems launched in London in 1990 and sold to corporations (Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi, Olin) before the 1991 arcade version.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: The Virtuality 1000SU VR system was launched in 1990 at the Computer Graphics ’90 exhibition held at Alexandra Palace in London.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: Many other systems were sold to corporations including Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi and Olin.

note: Original 1991 arcade release was preceded by the 1990 corporate-sale product. Military helmet simulators and VPL's 1980s RB2 could be earlier but no fetched page dated a real-purpose use, so not adopted.

what: World of Warcraft passed 10 million subscribers worldwide.

sources.title: World of Warcraft
sources.quote: On January 22, 2008, World of Warcraft had more than 10 million subscribers worldwide

note: Lineage (Korea) reported over 3 million subscribers at one point but no date could be verified; EverQuest (259k, 2000) and Ultima Online (250k peak, 2003) are far smaller. WoW's 2004 launch and 2005-06 sales suggest mass use began earlier, but 2008 is the only dated figure verified.
